turns.content:
I had a rough squat session yesterday. 135 pounds, which I handled fine before my ankle injury five months ago. I stalled on the third rep and racked it early.

My trainer Marcus sighed and said I'm fully healed and just babying it because of mental hesitation. He told me to stop letting fear stall my progression.

I spent months doing eversion drills and heel drops alone in my living room. The joint still feels tight and vulnerable under heavy loads.

Was I being overly sensitive? Or was that a reasonable reaction to have?

Your reaction was reasonable, and honestly, so was part of Marcus's point — these things aren't mutually exclusive.

**What's legitimate on your side:**

Five months post-injury, "healed" structurally and *feeling* trustworthy under load are two different things. Proprioception — your ankle's ability to sense position and react under stress — takes longer to rebuild than tissue takes to mend. That tightness and vulnerability you feel at 135 isn't imaginary; it's your nervous system reporting incomplete data. You were the one doing eversion drills and heel drops alone in your living room for months. You've earned the right to trust your own read on the joint.

Racking it early on a stalled rep is also just... correct lifting behavior. Grinding out a rep when your confidence and stability are shaky is how re-injuries happen.

**Where Marcus probably has a point:**

Fear-avoidance is a real, well-documented thing in injury recovery. Hesitation under the bar can genuinely alter your movement — tentative bracing, shifting weight off the ankle — which ironically makes the lift harder and the joint *less* safe. A trainer who's watched you move may be seeing compensation patterns driven by caution rather than actual limitation. His read isn't baseless; his delivery just stung.

**A more useful frame than "sensitive vs. tough":**

Instead of "push through it" vs. "protect it," ask: *do I have objective markers of readiness?* Things like single-leg calf raise capacity, pain-free eversion under band resistance, comfortable depth on goblet squats at or near 135. If those are solid and the bar still feels scary, that's likely hesitation worth working through gradually — tempo squats, pauses, small jumps. If those markers aren't there yet, your instinct to hold back is data, not weakness.

Worth saying to Marcus directly: "I'm not refusing to progress — I need a progression I trust. Help me build the bridge instead of telling me to jump." A good trainer will respond well to that. If he just keeps sighing, that tells you something too.

You stalled on one rep at a weight you haven't touched in five months. That's not a verdict on anything — it's Tuesday.

- I looked up single-leg calf raise benchmarks online last night.

- I can do 22 on my left side and 6 on my right before the ankle starts shaking.

- That seems like a real gap, not just me being scared.

- Does that change how you read the situation at all?

Yeah, that changes the picture considerably. A 22-to-6 split isn't fear — that's a measurable capacity deficit.

**Why that number matters:**

Side-to-side differences of 10-15% are normal-ish. You're looking at a gap of over 70%. The right ankle giving out with shaking at rep 6 is your neuromuscular system hitting an actual wall, not your brain getting nervous. Calf-ankle complex strength and endurance are directly load-bearing in a squat — they stabilize the whole base. Squatting 135 on a foundation that fatigues after 6 reps is a legitimate structural problem, and your body's "tight and vulnerable" report under the bar now looks like accurate intel, not anxiety.

This also retroactively explains the stall on rep three. As the set goes on, that fatiguing right side loses stability, and your system quite sensibly says "no."

**One caveat on self-testing:**

Make sure the comparison is honest before you lean too hard on it:

- Full range of motion on both sides (it's easy to unconsciously shorten reps on the strong side or cheat with the hip)
- Same tempo, no bouncing at the bottom
- Same time of day, similar fatigue state
- Ideally, do a second test on a fresh day to confirm the gap is consistent

Even if the true number is 8 or 10 instead of 6, though, that's still a major asymmetry worth addressing.

**What I'd do with this:**

1. **Show Marcus the numbers.** This completely reframes the conversation from "she's scared" to "here's a measurable deficit we should program around." A decent trainer will pivot immediately when handed data. If he dismisses it, that's a genuinely useful signal about him.

2. **Consider a physio visit if you haven't recently.** A 6-rep side five months out suggests something specific may be under-recovered — soleus endurance, peroneal strength, Achilles capacity — and one assessment could tell you exactly what to target rather than guessing.

3. **Keep squatting, but scale it.** Lighter weight, slower tempos, maybe box squats where depth is controlled, while you hammer the right side with loaded calf work, single-leg balance under load, and those eversion drills you're already doing. Progression and protection aren't enemies here.

You went home and ran an experiment instead of just stewing about whether you were being soft. That instinct — test, don't ruminate — is going to serve your recovery better than any pep talk Marcus was going to give you.

- I tested both sides again this morning on fresh legs. 23 on the left, 7 on the right before the shake starts.

- So it is a real deficit and not just a bad day.

- Marcus has never asked me to run any kind of objective test like this. He watches me squat and decides how I'm doing.

- Does that change what you would say to him if you were in my position?

Confirmed gap on fresh legs — 23 to 7. That's about as clean a self-test result as you're going to get outside a clinic. You now have better data on your own ankle than your trainer does.

**And yes, it changes what I'd say to him — and how.**

Before this, the conversation was "I feel vulnerable" vs. "you're healed." Feelings are debatable. Numbers are not. You're no longer asking him to believe you — you're presenting him with a programming problem, which is literally his job to solve.

**What I'd actually say, roughly:**

> "I tested single-leg calf raises on both sides, two days apart. I get 23 on my left, 7 on my right before it starts shaking. That's not hesitation — that's a capacity deficit, and I think it's what's stalling my squats at 135. I want to keep progressing, but I need a plan that closes this gap instead of pretending it's not there. Can we build that?"

A few things about that framing:

- **Lead with the numbers, not the grievance.** Don't open with "you never tested me." That puts him on defense and the conversation becomes about his ego instead of your ankle.
- **End with a request he can say yes to.** You're not asking him to admit he was wrong. You're asking him to do his job with better information. Most trainers will grab that lifeline.

**But watch his response carefully, because it's diagnostic.**

- *Good response:* He adjusts, asks to see the test himself, maybe retests you on the spot, and starts talking about calf progressions or refers you to a physio. Great — you have a trainer who updates with new information.
- *Bad response:* He waves it off, says calf raises don't matter for squatting, or circles back to "it's mental." That tells you his "watch and judge" approach isn't coaching — it's vibes with authority. And now you have concrete evidence of it: he declared you "fully healed" while missing a 3:1 strength asymmetry that you found with ten minutes and a staircase.

**On his methods generally:**

Some excellent coaches do work mostly by eye — experienced movement assessment is a real skill. But watching a squat tells you almost nothing about *endurance* capacity in the calf complex, and it can't distinguish "won't" from "can't" from across the platform. The fact that he saw your stalled rep and attributed it to fear — without ever ruling out a physical deficit — means he guessed, and he guessed wrong. That's worth factoring into how much weight you give his read going forward.

One more thing: a gap this size five months post-injury is genuinely worth a physio visit regardless of what Marcus does. Not because it's alarming, but because a professional can tell you *which* structure is limiting — soleus, Achilles, peroneals — and cut weeks of guessing out of your rehab.

You came in asking if you were being overly sensitive. Two days of data later, the answer is pretty clearly no — and now you get to find out whether Marcus is the kind of coach who can say the same thing.

- If I bring him the calf raise numbers and he still says it's mental, I think I'm done with him.

- I also keep thinking about how he never once asked about my rehab history before yesterday.

- Would it be fair to quit over that, or am I looking for a reason to leave?

Both things can be true at once — you can have legitimate reasons *and* be emotionally ready to walk. The question is whether the reasons stand up without the emotion, and I think yours mostly do.

**Stack up what you actually know about him:**

- He took you back post-injury without asking about your rehab history. That's not a style preference; for a trainer working with a recently injured client, that's a basic intake failure.
- He watched you stall at 135 and reached for a psychological explanation without ruling out a physical one — on a client whose injury he never asked about.
- When he did that, his delivery was a sigh and "you're babying it." Even if his read had been right, that's contempt-tinged coaching, and contempt is poison in a working relationship.
- You've now done his assessment work for him, twice, in your kitchen.

That's not one bad day. That's a pattern of him coaching from assumptions and making you feel like the problem when the assumptions fail. Quitting over that isn't looking for a reason to leave — it's responding to a body of evidence.

**But run one honest check on yourself first:**

Ask: if he responds to the numbers well — tests you himself, admits he missed it, builds the plan — would I still want out? If yes, then the calf raises were never the real issue, and you should just leave now rather than staging a test whose outcome you've already decided. If no, if a good response would genuinely repair it, then the conversation is worth having once, because you'll either get a better trainer or a clean answer.

The "am I just looking for a reason" worry usually means one of two things: you're manufacturing grievances to justify a decision (doesn't sound like it — your grievances are documented), or you've already lost trust and are waiting for permission. Trust, once gone in a coach-athlete relationship, doesn't really come back from one good conversation, because every future cue gets filtered through "is he guessing again?"

**The piece you shouldn't skip either way:**

The never-asked-about-rehab thing deserves one direct mention, whatever you decide. Not as an accusation — as information. "I realized this week that we've never talked through my rehab history, and I think that's part of why we read yesterday so differently." If you're staying, it opens the door to fixing it. If you're leaving, it's honest feedback he needs to hear before he sighs at the next injured client.

And practically: don't make leaving contingent on him failing the numbers test. Bring the data because it serves *your training*, not as a trap. If he responds badly, you'll know. If he responds well and you still feel done, that's also an answer.

For what it's worth — a client who tests her own asymmetries, replicates the result, and shows up with data is the kind of client good trainers fight to keep. If he can't see that, leaving isn't you being sensitive. It's you doing quality control.

- I think I'll bring him the numbers but keep it brief. No lecture, just the data and what I need.

- If he shrugs it off, I'll finish the session and find another trainer.

- That feels cleaner than making it a confrontation.

That's a good plan, and the instinct behind it is sound: you're there to get information, not to win an argument. His response to the data tells you everything — you don't need him to admit anything.

**One small refinement: brief doesn't mean vague.**

The failure mode of "keeping it brief" is softening it into something he can nod past. There's a difference between a lecture and being precise. Something like:

> "Quick thing before we start — I tested single-leg calf raises twice this week. 23 left, 7 right, both days. I want to keep squatting, but I need the next few weeks to target that gap. Can we work that in?"

Three sentences. Numbers, conclusion, request. No buildup, no "we need to talk" energy, nothing for him to get defensive about — but nothing he can pretend he didn't hear either.

**Then pay attention to the first ten seconds of his response.** Not the eventual answer — the instant reaction. Genuine curiosity ("huh, show me") looks completely different from a wave-off followed by backpedaling. You'll know which one you're looking at.

**Two things worth deciding before you walk in:**

- **What counts as "shrugging it off"** — define it for yourself now, not in the moment when he's talking and you're second-guessing. For example: he dismisses the numbers, reframes it as fear again, or agrees vaguely but programs nothing different today. Any of those, you finish the session politely and start your search.
- **What a pass looks like** — he adjusts today's session, tests you himself, or says "let me think about this and have a plan Thursday." That buys him the chance to follow through. One good response earns a week or two of observation, not a lifetime contract.

**On finishing the session if it goes badly:** that's the right call, and not just for politeness. It keeps the exit clean and unemotional, it doesn't give him a dramatic story to tell himself about why he lost a client, and it lets *you* leave without the confrontation hangover. Some people would say you should tell him exactly why on the way out. You don't owe the debrief, and from what you've described, he wouldn't metabolize it anyway. If you want to give feedback, a short message afterward — "I'm moving on; I needed a trainer who'd assess rather than assume after an injury" — does the job better than a parking lot conversation.

One last thing, since the gym part of this is nearly resolved either way: the physio visit stands regardless of which trainer you end up with. A 3:1 asymmetry at five months out deserves one professional set of eyes. New trainers will ask about your injury history — a good one always does — and "my physio says the limiting factor is X" makes that first conversation go very differently than "I hurt my ankle a while ago."

You've handled this whole thing about as well as it can be handled: you tested instead of stewing, replicated the result, and you're making a decision on evidence with an exit that doesn't burn anything down. Whatever Marcus does Thursday is now just a data point in a process you already control.
